plate_findings.evidence: Caption identifies irregular curvilinear and trabecular woven bone characteristic of fibrous dysplasia.
Caption explicitly describes an inconspicuous or absent osteoblastic rim around the C-shaped trabecula.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Patient H&E micrograph showing irregular curvilinear woven bone trabeculae in a fibroblastic background, a characteristic histologic manifestation of fibrous dysplasia. B: Patient H&E micrograph showing the characteristic curvilinear C-shaped woven bone trabecula with inconspicuous osteoblastic rimming. C: Patient H&E micrograph with arrow-marked rounded, concentric psammoma-like calcifications in fibrous tissue, a captioned histologic feature of fibrous dysplasia. D: Patient H&E micrograph showing hyaline cartilage nodules touching fibrous tissue, with possible endochondral calcification as specifically described in the caption for fibrous dysplasia.

panels.figure_caption: Fibrous dysplasia histology. Microscopic view of fibrous dysplasia: (A) Irregular curvilinear and trabecular woven bone in a bland fibroblastic background (H&E, 4×). (B) Curvilinear, C-shaped bone trabecula with an inconspicuous osteoblastic rim is characteristic (H&E, 10×). (C) Rounded, concentric (psammoma-like) calcifications are present within fibrous tissue (arrows) (H&E, 10×). (D) Nodules of hyaline cartilage can be seen touching fibrous tissue. These can undergo endochondral calcification (H&E, 4×).
in_text_mentions: At the microarchitectural scale, FD is characterized by inhibition of trabeculae formation and organization. The trabeculae that are formed are typically thin, discontinuous, and surrounded by abundant fibrous tissue (Figure 12). Consequently, there is a limited bone response at the microarchitectural scale to applied stress. Overall, bone and bone marrow in FD are converted into an architecturally disorganized and mechanically unsound fibro-osseous tissue [58].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Radiograph of humerus showing endosteal resorption, cortical thinning, and fibro-osseous matrix replacement consistent with fibrous dysplasia. B: Radiograph of proximal femur showing medullary canal replacement by fibro-osseous matrix and endosteal resorption consistent with fibrous dysplasia.
panels.attribution_text: Littman et al. The GNAS Gene: Fibrous Dysplasia, McCune-Albright Syndrome, and Skeletal Structure and Function.. Genes 2025. doi:10.3390/genes16111360. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 14.
panels.figure_caption: Radiographs of a patient with fibrous dysplasia. (A) The humerus exhibits a wide medullary canal with endosteal resorption and very thin cortices. Heterogeneous medullary patterns indicate fibro-osseous matrix with prominent lytic areas. (B) The proximal femur displays faint compressive trabeculae in the femoral head and neck and replacement of the trabecular bone. Replacement of the medullary canal with fibro-osseous matrix can be observed, especially in the inter- and sub-trochanteric areas (asterisk). Extensive endosteal resorption is apparent. Images displayed with patient consent.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Whole-body 18F-NaF PET image from a 23-year-old patient showing extensive multifocal skeletal uptake characteristic of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. [raw subtype: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia] B: T1-weighted, FLAIR, and STIR MRI sequences demonstrate craniofacial and skull-base FD involvement in the same 23-year-old patient. [raw subtype: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia with craniofacial involvement] C: Whole-body 18F-NaF PET image from a 53-year-old patient shows pronounced craniofacial FD activity with limited involvement elsewhere. [raw subtype: craniofacial-predominant fibrous dysplasia] D: T1-weighted, FLAIR, and STIR MRI sequences show extensive craniofacial FD in the nasal bones with distortion of the sinus cavity in a 53-year-old patient. [raw subtype: extensive craniofacial fibrous dysplasia]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Plain radiograph of the hip in a pediatric patient with fibrous dysplasia, demonstrating the classic ground-glass matrix of the intramedullary FD lesion in the proximal femur, with no visible fracture as noted in the caption. B: Reformatted CT image of the proximal femur clearly demonstrating a pathologic fracture through the fibrous dysplasia lesion in the medial proximal femur, as explicitly described in the figure caption with corresponding arrow annotation. C: 3D reformatted CT image of the proximal femur showing the pathologic fracture through the fibrous dysplasia lesion, consistent with the other reformatted CT panels in Figure 8 used to detect subtle fractures in FD. D: Coronal reformatted CT image of the proximal femur showing the pathologic fracture through the fibrous dysplasia lesion, consistent with the other reformatted CT panels in Figure 8 used to detect subtle fractures in FD.

panels.figure_caption: CT for detecting subtle fractures. A) This radiograph was from a 9-year-old boy who complained of new-onset, focal pain in the groin. No discernable fracture is apparent. B) Reformatted CT images of the lesion revealed a fracture in the medial proximal femur (arrows).
in_text_mentions: r the diagnosis of FD in the axial and appendicular skeleton (the axial skeleton is comprised of bones of the skull, hyoid bone, vertebra, sternum and ribs; the appendicular skeleton includes the hip, pelvic bone and the shoulder girdle (clavicle and scapula) (Fig. 2). However, x-rays are often unable to detect new, small microfractures. When new focal pain develops in an FD lesion and no fracture is evident on plain radiograph, CT and or MRI can be useful for detecting subtle fractures (Fig. 8). The classic lesion of the proximal femur in FD, the shepherd's crook deformity is common (Fig. 2).

plate_findings.evidence: In-text description of the lesions shown in Fig. 3A includes hypodense areas with a "ground glass appearance".
CT visibly shows expansile dysplastic osseous involvement, and the caption identifies bone lesions caused by polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.
The 3D craniofacial CT reconstruction visibly demonstrates dysplastic craniofacial bony enlargement and distortion in the maxillary region.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a patient CT demonstrating craniofacial osseous lesions attributable by the caption and accompanying in-text description to polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, including the characteristic ground-glass matrix. [raw subtype: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia associated with McCune-Albright syndrome] B: Panel B contains craniofacial CT views from the patient and specifically documents severe maxillary fibrous dysplasia with total maxillary sinus aplasia. The osseous craniofacial distortion supports a configured fibrous-dysplasia finding, while the sinus aplasia is retained as a proposed finding because it is absent from the allowed vocabulary. [raw subtype: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia associated with McCune-Albright syndrome]

panels.figure_caption: Bilateral proximal femoral deformity with a ground-glass appearance.
in_text_mentions: ydroxyproline levels were higher, indicating increased bone turnover. The blood count, electrocardiogram, and serum liver enzymes were all within normal limits. There were no signs of precocious puberty; however, the TSH level in the serum was high. Based on a retrospective evaluation, a history of a wide-based gait with minimum to no activity restriction was obtained. The skeletal survey revealed bilateral short deformed tubular metacarpal bones (Figure 3), as well as a bilateral proximal femoral deformity with a ground-glass appearance (Figure 4), with no scoliosis or craniofacial asymmetry.
